--- title: "Tool 1 — The Model-Free Ladder" subtitle: "Pearson · Spearman · Distance Correlation" --- *Learn-the-tool track · Lab 1 of 3.* This lab walks the **no-density road** — the measures that compare two return series $X$ and $Y$ straight from the samples, never needing to first estimate a probability distribution — up one ladder: the *idea* (three measures, one template) stays fixed while the **data grows up under it**, from a toy whose answer you can check by hand to the real basket of stocks. Along the way two *gaps between the measures* turn out to flag two different dangers. **What you will produce:** a watchlist of real stock pairs that crash together harder than the cheap tools let on — the candidates to hand to the tail-risk job. --- ## 🧪 Rung 1 · Toy — Known Answer Start where the truth is not in doubt. `datasets.nonlinear_dependence()` draws $y = x^2 + \text{noise}$ on a range centered at zero: **$y$ is almost entirely fixed once you know $x$** — about as dependent as two variables can be — yet the relationship is symmetric (the same $y$ for $+x$ and $-x$), so a *linear* measure like Pearson must read $\approx 0$. That gap between "obviously dependent" and "Pearson says nothing" is the whole reason this road climbs past Pearson, and here we can check the answer by eye. ::: {#d0b42d52 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # y = x² + noise (y is ~determined by x, but the link is symmetric) x_toy: Float[Array, "n"] y_toy: Float[Array, "n"] x_toy, y_toy = datasets.nonlinear_dependence(n=1000, noise=0.05, seed=0) print(f"x: {x_toy.shape} y = x² + noise (y is ~determined by x)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` x: (1000,) y = x² + noise (y is ~determined by x) ``` ::: ::: **The algorithm — one template, three transforms.** Every measure on this road has the shape `compare(transform(x), transform(y))`: ``` Pearson = corr( x , y ) # transform = identity Spearman = corr( rank x , rank y ) # transform = rank distance corr = corr( Ã , B̃ ) # Ã, B̃ = double-centered |distances| ``` The first two are one line. The third needs the **distance transform**: turn each point into its vector of distances to every other point, double-center the matrix, and correlate. Spelled out with the axes visible: ::: {#878cb194 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} def centered_distances(z: Float[Array, "n"]) -> Float[Array, "n n"]: """The dCor transform: double-centered pairwise distances. Dᵢⱼ = |zᵢ - zⱼ| [same units as z] Ãᵢⱼ = Dᵢⱼ - D̄ᵢ. - D̄.ⱼ + D̄.. (row, column, grand means removed) """ D: Float[Array, "n n"] = np.abs(einx.subtract("i, j -> i j", z, z)) # Dᵢⱼ = |zᵢ - zⱼ| row_mean: Float[Array, "n"] = einx.mean("i j -> i", D) # D̄ᵢ. — point i's mean distance col_mean: Float[Array, "n"] = einx.mean("i j -> j", D) # D̄.ⱼ A: Float[Array, "n n"] = einx.subtract("i j, i -> i j", D, row_mean) # remove row mean A = einx.subtract("i j, j -> i j", A, col_mean) # remove column mean return A + D.mean() # add back the grand mean D̄.. # dCor² is the correlation of the centered-distance entries — verify the identity: A: Float[Array, "n n"] = centered_distances(x_toy) B: Float[Array, "n n"] = centered_distances(y_toy) corr_entries = pearsonr(A.ravel(), B.ravel())[0] # corr(Ã, B̃) over all n² entries print(f"corr(Ã, B̃) over all n² entries = {corr_entries:.4f}") print(f"dCor² = {distance_correlation(x_toy, y_toy) ** 2:.4f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` corr(Ã, B̃) over all n² entries = 0.2348 dCor² = 0.2348 ``` ::: ::: Now run all three and read them against what we *know* is there: ::: {#472f00d6 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} t_toy = measure_trio(x_toy, y_toy) nonlin_gap = t_toy["distance"] - abs(t_toy["spearman"]) # dCor − |Spearman| — what the distance step adds print(f"Pearson = {t_toy['pearson']:+.3f} (linear — blind to the symmetry)") print(f"Spearman = {t_toy['spearman']:+.3f} (monotone — also blind)") print(f"distance = {t_toy['distance']:.3f} (sees the dependence)") print(f"\ndCor − |Spearman| = {nonlin_gap:+.3f} ← the non-monotone gap") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pearson = +0.030 (linear — blind to the symmetry) Spearman = +0.070 (monotone — also blind) distance = 0.485 (sees the dependence) dCor − |Spearman| = +0.415 ← the non-monotone gap ``` ::: ::: ::: {#fig-toy-distance-compute .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Sort by x and thin out, so the distance matrices read as smooth images. order: Float[Array, "m"] = np.argsort(x_toy)[::3] xs: Float[Array, "m"] = x_toy[order] ys: Float[Array, "m"] = y_toy[order] Dx: Float[Array, "m m"] = np.abs(einx.subtract("i, j -> i j", xs, xs)) # |xᵢ - xⱼ| Dy: Float[Array, "m m"] = np.abs(einx.subtract("i, j -> i j", ys, ys)) # |yᵢ - yⱼ| ``` ::: ::: {#cell-fig-toy-distance .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, (ax0, ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12.5, 4.0)) ax0.scatter(xs, ys, s=12, c=WARM, alpha=0.55, edgecolors="none") ax0.set_title("the U-shape (sorted by x)", fontsize=11) despine(ax0) for ax, M, ttl, cmap in [(ax1, Dx, "pairwise distances in X", "Blues"), (ax2, Dy, "pairwise distances in Y", "Oranges")]: ax.imshow(M, cmap=cmap, origin="lower") ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=11) for ax in (ax0, ax1, ax2): ax.set_xticks([]) ax.set_yticks([]) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The U-shape and its distance transform (points sorted by x, every 3rd kept for a readable matrix). The X-distances form a smooth gradient; the Y-distances show the U as a cross — points on opposite arms have similar y. Distance correlation is the correlation of these two patterns; Pearson and Spearman on the raw values see almost nothing.](lab-tool1-ladder_files/figure-html/fig-toy-distance-output-1.png){#fig-toy-distance width=1455 height=464} ::: ::: The known answer holds: the two cheap measures read $\approx 0$, distance correlation does not. The **`dCor − Spearman` gap** is the tell-tale sign of *non-monotone* dependence — a link where $y$ does not simply rise or fall with $x$. That is the first of the two gaps this lab tracks. --- ## 🎭 Rung 2 · Toy-Real — A Stylized Market $y = x^2$ never happens in markets. What *does* is **joint crashes**: two banks that drift together on calm days and plunge together on the bad ones. `datasets.two_banks()` is that stylized picture — a shared driving factor plus a ~10% set of days where both names fall hard at once (the `crash_mask`). Here both banks move the same way (both fall together), so Spearman already catches the link and the `dCor − Spearman` gap stays shut. The crash days are instead a handful of huge moves that show up in both banks at once — *outliers* — and **Pearson gives them too much weight**, opening a *second* gap, `Pearson − Spearman`, precisely on those days. ::: {#61b23cdf .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} a: Float[Array, "n_days"] b: Float[Array, "n_days"] crash: Float[Array, "n_days"] # boolean mask of co-crash days a, b, crash = datasets.two_banks(n=1500, seed=0) print(f"{int(crash.sum())} crash days of {crash.size} ({crash.mean():.0%})\n") def tail_gap(m: dict) -> float: """How far Pearson runs ahead of Spearman — the heavy-joint-tail fingerprint.""" return m["pearson"] - m["spearman"] # P − S: ranks cap outliers; raw Pearson does not all_days = measure_trio(a, b) calm_only = measure_trio(a[~crash], b[~crash]) # the same pair, crash days removed print(" Pearson Spearman distance Pearson−Spearman") print(f"all days {all_days['pearson']:+.3f} {all_days['spearman']:+.3f} " f"{all_days['distance']:.3f} {tail_gap(all_days):+.3f}") print(f"calm only {calm_only['pearson']:+.3f} {calm_only['spearman']:+.3f} " f"{calm_only['distance']:.3f} {tail_gap(calm_only):+.3f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 160 crash days of 1500 (11%) Pearson Spearman distance Pearson−Spearman all days +0.894 +0.838 0.844 +0.056 calm only +0.799 +0.778 0.748 +0.021 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-twobanks .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.0)) ax.scatter(a[~crash], b[~crash], s=12, c=COOL, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none", label="calm days") ax.scatter(a[crash], b[crash], s=26, c=CRASH, alpha=0.9, edgecolors="none", label="crash days") ax.set_xlabel("bank A return") ax.set_ylabel("bank B return") ax.set_title("Crash days inflate Pearson; the ranks shrug", fontsize=11.5) ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper left") despine(ax) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The stylized bank pair, crash days highlighted. The calm cloud is roughly elliptical — where all three measures agree — but the red crash days in the lower-left corner are huge co-moving outliers. They lift the magnitude-sensitive Pearson more than the rank-based Spearman, so the Pearson − Spearman gap opens on exactly these days.](lab-tool1-ladder_files/figure-html/fig-twobanks-output-1.png){#fig-twobanks width=752 height=585} ::: ::: Two readings. First, all three measures are **high and close together** — the two banks move the same way, so the cheap tools already capture the link; you do *not* need the top of the ladder here. Second, adding the crash days back lifts Pearson far more than Spearman: Spearman works on ranks, so the biggest crash counts only as "the most extreme day," whereas Pearson multiplies the raw return sizes, so a huge crash pulls it up sharply. That widening `Pearson − Spearman` gap is the fingerprint of a **heavy joint tail** — two names that crash together far more violently than their calm-day relationship suggests. That is the signal we now hunt on the real book of stocks. --- ## 📈 Rung 3 · Real — The Full Basket Now the real data. We **reload** the prepared daily returns — there is no cleaning here; the steps that turn raw prices into log-returns live in [the data primer](../../data/01-downloading-and-parsing.qmd) — show a corner of the table, and run the *same* `measure_trio` on every pair of stocks. We are looking for the same two gaps as before, now across all the real pairs: which pairs have a non-monotone link (`d − S`), and which hide a heavy joint tail (`P − S`). ::: {#353e8be3 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} R = datasets.load_returns() # prepared 14-name daily panel META = datasets.load_basket_meta() label = dict(zip(META["ticker"], META["label"])) sector = dict(zip(META["ticker"], META["sector"])) tickers = list(R.columns) print(f"{len(R)} trading days × {len(tickers)} stocks " f"({R.index.min().date()} → {R.index.max().date()})") R.iloc[:3, :6].round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 4778 trading days × 14 stocks (2007-01-04 → 2025-12-30) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}
JPM BAC C WFC GS AAPL
date
2007-01-04 0.0025 0.0064 -0.0034 0.0017 -0.0094 0.0220
2007-01-05 -0.0083 -0.0080 -0.0053 -0.0056 0.0010 -0.0071
2007-01-08 0.0033 0.0039 0.0051 -0.0028 0.0232 0.0049
``` ::: ::: Distance correlation builds an $n \times n$ matrix, which gets expensive on the full history, so we take **one** lab-local shortcut — pick a random ~600 days for that one measure (the order of the days does not matter for measuring dependence) — then sort the pairs by strength and report **both** gaps: ::: {#d8c18463 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} import itertools Rs = R.sample(600, random_state=0) # subsample only for the O(n²) distance corr rows = [] for x_t, y_t in itertools.combinations(tickers, 2): xf: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[x_t].values # full series — cheap measures yf: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[y_t].values xs_sub: Float[Array, "w"] = Rs[x_t].values # subsample — the n×n distance corr ys_sub: Float[Array, "w"] = Rs[y_t].values pear = pearsonr(xf, yf)[0] spear = spearmanr(xf, yf)[0] dist = distance_correlation(xs_sub, ys_sub) rows.append(dict(pair=f"{x_t}/{y_t}", same_sector=(sector[x_t] == sector[y_t]), pearson=pear, spearman=spear, distance=dist, tail=pear - spear, # P − S: heavy-joint-tail flag → Job C nonlin=dist - abs(spear))) # dCor − |Spearman|: non-monotone flag → Tool 2 rows.sort(key=lambda r: r["distance"], reverse=True) # rank by dependence strength print(f"{'pair':<11s}{'Pears':>7s}{'Spear':>7s}{'dist':>7s}{'P−S':>7s}{'d−S':>7s} sector") print("-" * 53) for r in rows[:8]: print(f"{r['pair']:<11s}{r['pearson']:>+7.3f}{r['spearman']:>+7.3f}" f"{r['distance']:>7.3f}{r['tail']:>+7.3f}{r['nonlin']:>+7.3f}" f" {'✓' if r['same_sector'] else ''}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` pair Pears Spear dist P−S d−S sector ----------------------------------------------------- JPM/BAC +0.829 +0.813 0.817 +0.015 +0.003 ✓ BAC/C +0.820 +0.794 0.808 +0.026 +0.014 ✓ XOM/CVX +0.856 +0.826 0.793 +0.030 -0.033 ✓ JPM/GS +0.770 +0.761 0.783 +0.008 +0.022 ✓ DUK/SO +0.822 +0.785 0.783 +0.038 -0.002 ✓ JPM/WFC +0.823 +0.780 0.781 +0.043 +0.000 ✓ JPM/C +0.763 +0.772 0.779 -0.009 +0.007 ✓ BAC/WFC +0.825 +0.768 0.762 +0.058 -0.006 ✓ ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## Where This Data Comes From The panel, its sectors, and the co-crash structure these pairs ride on are laid bare in the data primer — [From Raw Prices to a Clean Panel](../../data/01-downloading-and-parsing.qmd) and [Co-Movement & Co-Crashes](../../data/04-co-movement-and-co-crashes.qmd). This lab reloads that panel and never re-derives it. ::: Read the two gap columns. `d − S` (the non-monotone flag) is **near zero everywhere** — daily stock pairs move the same way, so the U-shape problem of Rung 1 simply does not arise on this book. `P − S` (the heavy-tail flag) is the interesting one, and it does *not* simply follow dependence strength: the most strongly linked pairs (the bank pairs sitting on top) carry only a small gap, because both of their numbers are already high. The largest `P − S` values, as the watchlist below shows, belong to other pairs. --- ## 💰 Rung 4 · Application — Which Pairs Hide a Heavy Joint Tail The deliverable is a **watchlist**: the pairs with the largest `Pearson − Spearman` gap. A positive gap means a few extreme days where both names move together are pulling Pearson (which reacts to the size of each move) up, while Spearman (which only looks at ranks) ignores them — a cheap fingerprint of a **heavy joint tail**, and one we found without assuming any model for the returns. The surprise is *which* pairs top the list: not the banks (already tightly linked on every kind of day), but **cross-sector** pairs — utilities and energy against the rest — that look only weakly related in calm times yet get dragged down together in 2008 and 2020. Those are the diversification illusions: pairs that look safe to hold side by side until the crisis hits. They are exactly what to hand to [Job C · Hidden Risk](lab-jobC-hidden-risk.qmd), whose measure looks specifically at crash days to test the tail properly — something none of the all-days measures on this road can do. ::: {#fig-watchlist-compute .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} flagged = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r["tail"], reverse=True)[:12] # the 12 heaviest P − S tails print(f"top {len(flagged)} pairs by Pearson − Spearman → hand to Job C\n") print(f"{'pair':<11s}{'Pearson':>9s}{'Spearman':>10s}{'P−S':>8s} sector") print("-" * 46) for r in flagged: print(f"{r['pair']:<11s}{r['pearson']:>+9.3f}{r['spearman']:>+10.3f}" f"{r['tail']:>+8.3f} {'same' if r['same_sector'] else 'cross'}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` top 12 pairs by Pearson − Spearman → hand to Job C pair Pearson Spearman P−S sector ---------------------------------------------- CVX/DUK +0.419 +0.276 +0.143 cross XOM/DUK +0.423 +0.289 +0.134 cross GS/DUK +0.322 +0.193 +0.129 cross XOM/SO +0.408 +0.280 +0.127 cross CVX/SO +0.392 +0.265 +0.126 cross C/DUK +0.296 +0.181 +0.115 cross MSFT/DUK +0.338 +0.226 +0.112 cross AAPL/DUK +0.272 +0.160 +0.112 cross JPM/DUK +0.337 +0.226 +0.111 cross MSFT/CVX +0.443 +0.336 +0.108 cross BAC/DUK +0.286 +0.179 +0.107 cross WFC/DUK +0.316 +0.214 +0.101 cross ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-watchlist .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} top = flagged[::-1] # smallest gap at the bottom of the bars fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 4.0)) colors = [COOL if r["same_sector"] else CRASH for r in top] ax.barh([r["pair"] for r in top], [r["tail"] for r in top], color=colors) ax.set_xlabel("Pearson − Spearman (the cheap tool over-reads the tail)") ax.set_title("Watchlist — heaviest joint tails first", fontsize=12) despine(ax) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The watchlist: the 12 real pairs with the largest Pearson − Spearman gap. Each is a pair whose extreme co-moving days inflate the linear number — a model-free fingerprint of joint-tail risk, and the triage queue for the tail job. Cross-sector pairs (red) dominate — utilities and energy coupling to the rest only in the tail, the diversification illusions; the strongly-coupled within-sector pairs (blue) carry a smaller gap.](lab-tool1-ladder_files/figure-html/fig-watchlist-output-1.png){#fig-watchlist width=896 height=465} ::: ::: Read the list as a priority queue: the largest gaps are pairs that are linked mainly through their shared crises, where Pearson most overstates how related they are on ordinary days. Hand them to Job C for the crash-day test. The *non-monotone* candidates instead (a large `d − S`, rare on this book) belong to [Tool 2 (mutual information)](lab-tool2-information.qmd) — mutual information is a measure that counts how much knowing one variable tells you about the other, in **bits**. --- ## Confirm It — The Gap *Is* the Crashes The watchlist is only as good as its premise: that the `Pearson − Spearman` gap really is caused by the shared crashes. Let us check it directly by **reloading the real crash days** — the worst 10% of days for the average bank, defined once in [Crashes & Drawdowns](../../data/03-crashes-and-drawdowns.qmd) — and re-running the Rung 2 split on the top flagged pair. If the premise holds, dropping the crash days should shrink the gap. ::: {#5afc8a70 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} worst = flagged[0] # the heaviest-tail pair t1, t2 = worst["pair"].split("/") bank_avg = R[["JPM", "BAC", "C", "WFC", "GS"]].mean(axis=1) # systemic factor = mean bank return crash: Float[Array, "n_days"] = (bank_avg <= bank_avg.quantile(0.10)).to_numpy() # worst 10% of bank days xr: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[t1].to_numpy() yr: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[t2].to_numpy() gap_all = pearsonr(xr, yr)[0] - spearmanr(xr, yr)[0] # P − S, all days gap_calm = pearsonr(xr[~crash], yr[~crash])[0] - spearmanr(xr[~crash], yr[~crash])[0] # P − S, crashes dropped shrink = 100 * (gap_all - gap_calm) / gap_all # % of the gap the crashes carried print(f"{worst['pair']} Pearson − Spearman gap") print(f" all days {gap_all:+.3f}") print(f" crash days removed {gap_calm:+.3f} ← {shrink:.0f}% of the gap was the crises") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` CVX/DUK Pearson − Spearman gap all days +0.143 crash days removed +0.104 ← 27% of the gap was the crises ``` ::: ::: Drop the market-wide crashes and roughly a third of the gap goes with them — the same drop `two_banks` showed in Rung 2, now on a real cross-sector pair you would never have flagged by ordinary correlation alone. The model-free ladder has done its job: it found *where* to look. How many **bits** that crash-time link is actually worth — and whether there is dependence the cheapest tools cannot count at all — is the question [Tool 2 · Information Measures](lab-tool2-information.qmd) takes up next.
